::: {.lede}
EuroCOMP Lab pools knowledge and resources across the people and organisations

::: {.eyebrow}
Why introduce experimental evaluations?
:::

## You need evidence on what is actually worth funding

The EU is one of the world’s largest investors in innovation. Research and innovation got roughly a tenth of its €361 billion Cohesion Policy budget for 2021–2027. Yet regional gaps in innovation outcomes are holding back the EU’s competitiveness. To keep pace with global competitors, every euro invested needs to deliver more.

Cohesion policy programmes often do not learn as they go. But policies need to adapt as circumstances change. That means identifying challenges, testing solutions, and refining approaches.

::: {.gold-panel}
This is what we call **science-based adaptive delivery**: testing, learning, and
adjusting as you go.
:::

## Randomised controlled trials show what works and why

By comparing what happens with support to what would have happened without it, a randomised controlled trial shows whether a cohesion policy programme is really the reason things improved. A programme built this way can adjust as conditions change, instead of running on assumptions made once and never tested.

Piloting a new idea at small scale is the best way to test it. For this, the evaluation needs to be designed ex-ante, before the call for proposals launches.

## Think you already know what program works and whom to fund?

But…

Would they have succeeded without you?

Would someone else have gained more from the same euro?

If the answer is not a clear yes, you should consider introducing experimentation.

::: {.eyebrow}
What is an impact evaluation
:::

## But what is impact evaluation exactly?

::: {.gold-panel}
It allows us to answer the questions: what impact did this intervention have on regional
development, and how did different approaches change the outcome? For whom did it work
best, and under which conditions?
:::

To answer that, an impact evaluation isolates a program's actual effect from everything
else going on (economic trends, other policies, or the kinds of firms likely to apply in
the first place), rather than just describing what happened. It compares what actually
happened after introducing a program to what would have happened without it, the
counterfactual.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Not the same as M&E
M&E tracks whether a program is implemented as planned. Impact evaluation tests whether
it caused a real difference, compared to what would have happened without it.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Built in from day one
The comparison group, sample size, and data collection all depend on decisions made
before a program launches, not added on afterward.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Each one builds on the last
Each evaluation answers some questions and raises new ones, helping you understand your
regional market and design more impactful programs next time.
:::
:::
